body_markdown:
The[Bristol Fighter](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/the-bristol-fighter-never-got-the-chance-to-scrap/) , which bit the dust with Bristol Cars back in 2011, is being revived as the first step for the revitalized British firm.


When current Bristol owner Paul King bought the defunct carmaker in 2022, he also got drawings and chassis for the 2004 eight-liter V-10-powered Fighter supercoupe and has vowed to finish the production run with five new cars. Bringing back the Fighter will “complete an unfinished story,” says Bristol, before the company embarks on a new chapter.


“Bringing Bristol Cars back is about far more than reviving a name; it is about bringing back the spirit of a marque that has always stood apart,” says King. “Bristol has a remarkable story, from its roots in aviation and engineering to the extraordinary and exclusive cars it crafted. We want to honor that heritage while giving Bristol a future that is every bit as distinctive.”


Sam Frost


Sam Frost

For now, though, Bristol is focused on delivering a final squadron of Fighters, with the first example finished in black over a tan interior accessed by its gullwing doors. Under the hood is a 518-hp version of the V-10 engine from the Dodge Viper, although buyers can opt for an upgrade to 592 horses should the standard 212-mph top speed be insufficient.


2026 marks 80 years since the first Bristol was built, and the Fighter was certainly the most ambitious in its history. The hand-beaten, wind-cheating aluminum body and box-section chassis were the work of former Brabham F1 engineer Max Bostrom and cut through the air with a drag coefficient of 0.28. A six-speed gearbox was standard issue, although a four-speed auto was also an option. Presumably that will be the same deal with these final Fighters. Bristol says that it can build Fighters in right- or left-hand drive and that U.S. buyers will be able to import them under[Show or Display rules](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/this-jaguar-set-the-tone-for-importing-under-show-or-display/) .

King has recruited Richard Hackett, who was a close advisor to long-term owner Tony Crook, as Chairman. “With Richard Hackett returning to the company, we have brought together an exceptional combination of heritage, knowledge, engineering and craftsmanship,” says King.


“This is the beginning of Bristol’s return, and there is much more to come.”
